title: A China Strategy That Lasts
gist: Senator Bill Cassidy argues Congress, not the executive branch, must codify a durable, bipartisan U.S. trade strategy against China's state-directed overproduction and export dumping — via permanent customs enforcement (codifying the June 2026 executive order and passing his Customs Modernization Act), Western Hemisphere reshoring (the Americas Act), and a Foreign Pollution Fee that taxes China's lax environmental standards.

themes.theme: China's trade policy as a geopolitical weapon

insights.claim: Beijing uses trade not only to generate economic growth but as a deliberate geopolitical tool, integrating national security, economic security, energy policy, and environmental policy to attract investment, expand its industrial base, and support its military.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Frames Chinese trade policy as inseparable from its military-industrial buildup, arguing investors and policymakers should treat trade exposure to China as a strategic-security variable, not purely a commercial one.
insights.quote: For decades, Beijing has used trade not only as a means to generate economic growth but also as a geopolitical tool to attract investment, strengthen its industrial base, expand its economy, and support its military.

insights.claim: Chinese government policy has produced overproduction at home across sectors like automobiles, chemicals, and solar panels, pushing companies to export at low prices, flooding international markets and eroding the manufacturing bases of rival economies.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Directly names the three sectors — autos, chemicals, solar — most exposed to Chinese export-dumping pressure, a useful screen for sector-level tariff/trade-policy risk and for domestic manufacturers likely to seek protection.
insights.quote: In sectors as varied as automobiles, chemicals, and solar panels, the Chinese government’s policies have led to overproduction at home, which pushes companies to export at low prices, flooding international markets and undermining the manufacturing bases of rival economies.

insights.claim: The United States cannot win a long-term strategic competition with China as long as Beijing controls global manufacturing and supply chains.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Sets a hard strategic red line — supply-chain and manufacturing dominance — as the metric by which U.S.-China competition should be judged, relevant to industrial-policy and reshoring investment theses.
insights.quote: And the United States cannot win a long-term competition with China when Beijing controls global manufacturing and supply chains.

themes.theme: Congress, not the executive, should own the strategy

insights.claim: Congress, not the executive branch alone, must establish a durable China trade framework, because U.S. approach to China has shifted with each presidential administration and even within a single presidency, undermining long-term policy consistency.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Argues for statutory rather than executive-order-based China policy as more durable and less reversible by a future administration — a factor investors should weigh when assessing the permanence of any given round of China tariffs or export controls.
insights.quote: If the United States hopes to compete successfully with China in the coming decades, Congress—not the executive branch alone—must establish a durable framework that can outlast political cycles.

themes.theme: Closing the de minimis loophole and modernizing customs

insights.claim: Before Congress closed the de minimis loophole in July 2025, approximately four million packages a day — mostly from China — entered the United States duty-free and largely unscreened under the $800 exemption threshold, allowing counterfeit products, fentanyl-containing goods, and cheap consumer products to pour in.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Quantifies the prior scale of unscreened low-value Chinese imports (4 million packages/day) — a concrete baseline for assessing the impact of the loophole's closure on e-commerce platforms reliant on de minimis shipping (e.g., Shein, Temu-style models) into the U.S.
insights.quote: Because of this loophole, in 2024, approximately four million packages a day—mostly from China—entered the United States duty free and largely unscreened.

insights.claim: While the U.S. de minimis threshold was $800 before its repeal, American exporters sending goods to China faced tariffs on any individual-use product costing more than $6.90 and on commercial products worth more than $690.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Highlights a roughly 100-to-1 asymmetry between the former U.S. de minimis exemption ($800) and China's reciprocal thresholds ($6.90/$690) — concrete evidence of unequal market access cited to justify the loophole's closure and further reciprocity-based trade legislation.
insights.quote: Meanwhile, American exporters sending goods to China faced tariffs on any products for individual use costing more than $6.90 and on commercial products worth more than $690.00.

insights.claim: Congress should codify the June 2026 executive order — which increases bonding requirements on high-risk goods, restricts repeat customs violators, sets minimum penalty floors, and expands supply-chain reporting requirements — into permanent law so it cannot be reversed by a future administration.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, near-term legislative target (codifying the June 2026 executive order) that would materially raise compliance costs for importers relying on customs-enforcement gaps.
insights.quote: Congress should codify the June 2026 executive order to make these changes permanent.

insights.claim: Cassidy's Customs Modernization Act (introduced 2023) would replace paper-based customs processes with electronic filing, require online marketplaces to provide verified seller and transaction data, and let Customs and Border Protection use the same AI and advanced data analytics that the marketplaces themselves already use.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: A concrete pending bill (CMA) that, if passed, would materially raise compliance and screening burdens on Chinese-origin e-commerce sellers — worth tracking as a legislative catalyst for cross-border e-commerce and marketplace-platform risk.
insights.quote: The Customs Modernization Act, which I introduced in 2023, aims to replace paper-based customs processes with comprehensive electronic filing. It also requires online marketplaces to provide verified seller and transaction data.

themes.theme: Reshoring supply chains to the Western Hemisphere

insights.claim: Cassidy's Americas Act (introduced March 2024) would encourage near-shoring production within the Western Hemisphere as a trusted-partnership alternative to Chinese dominance, diversifying supply chains, strengthening regional economies, and improving U.S. access to critical minerals.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Identifies a concrete legislative vehicle for Western Hemisphere critical-minerals and manufacturing nearshoring, relevant for Latin American critical-minerals and industrial investment theses tied to U.S. supply-chain diversification.
insights.quote: The Americas Act, which I introduced in March 2024, offers one model for accomplishing this by encouraging a trading network in the Western Hemisphere built on trusted partnerships rather than Chinese dominance.

insights.claim: The Americas Act would create an Americas Investment Corporation, allowing the U.S. government to co-invest with private firms in regional infrastructure and industrial projects, positioned as a credible alternative to China's Belt and Road Initiative.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: A proposed U.S. blended-finance vehicle explicitly designed to compete with Belt and Road financing in Latin America — relevant for infrastructure investors watching U.S.-China competition for regional development financing.
insights.quote: Among the act’s most powerful financing tools is the creation of an Americas Investment Corporation, which would allow the U.S. government to invest alongside private firms in infrastructure and industrial projects important to U.S. national security.

themes.theme: Using environmental standards as trade leverage

insights.claim: China's refusal to enforce environmental standards common in the advanced industrialized world has lowered its production costs, drawing manufacturing to China and thereby strengthening its industrial base, economy, and military modernization — at a cost to the global environment.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Links weak Chinese environmental enforcement directly to its manufacturing cost advantage and, by extension, to its military buildup — a framing that supports carbon-border-style tariff legislation as a national-security tool, not just a climate one.
insights.quote: One way that China has reduced its manufacturing costs is by refusing to enforce environmental standards commonly accepted in the advanced industrialized world.

insights.claim: A 2014 study found that on any given day, as much as 24 percent of the sulfates measured in the western United States originated in China, and other research links Chinese-origin foreign pollution to thousands of premature U.S. deaths and billions of dollars in added medical costs annually.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete, if dated, transboundary pollution data point (24% of western U.S. sulfates from China) used to justify pollution-based trade tariffs — worth noting the source study is from 2014, over a decade old.
insights.quote: According to a 2014 study, on any given day, as much as 24 percent of the sulfates measured in the western United States originated in China.

insights.claim: According to the International Energy Agency, China produced more than 12 billion tons of carbon dioxide in 2024 — more than 2.5 times the emissions of the United States — making it the world's biggest carbon emitter.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: A hard, sourced 2024 emissions comparison (China >12 billion tons CO2, >2.5x the U.S.) directly supporting the case for carbon-based trade tariffs targeting China specifically.
insights.quote: China is also the world’s biggest carbon emitter: according to the International Energy Agency, in 2024, China produced more than 12 billion tons of carbon dioxide, more than 2.5 times that of the United States.

insights.claim: Cassidy's proposed Foreign Pollution Fee (introduced April 2025) would impose an import charge roughly equal to the cost a country saves by ignoring U.S.-equivalent emissions standards, with China — as the world's biggest polluter — paying the highest price; since absolute U.S. emissions have declined steadily since 2005, the fee's size would grow over time if that trend continues.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: A specific, self-escalating tariff mechanism tied to relative emissions performance — worth tracking as a potential new cost layer on Chinese-origin manufactured imports (autos, chemicals, solar) if enacted.
insights.quote: The Foreign Pollution Fee, which I proposed in April 2025, is one legislative solution to this imbalance. It would impose an import charge approximately equal to the cost saved by ignoring emission goals comparable to those required by the United States.

insights.claim: Cassidy argues the U.S. China strategy must extend beyond a single administration and work with like-minded partners including Australia, Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the European Union.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Names the specific allied coalition Cassidy sees as necessary for durable China trade strategy, relevant for tracking multilateral trade-enforcement coordination.
insights.quote: Achieving that objective requires a strategy that extends beyond a single administration and even beyond the United States by working with like-minded partners including Australia, Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the European Union.

insights.claim: Cassidy states the relevant legislation (Customs Modernization Act, Americas Act, Foreign Pollution Fee, codification of the June 2026 executive order) has already been written and introduced; what is missing is the political will in Congress to pass it into law.
insights.speaker: Bill Cassidy
insights.so_what: Signals that the legislative pathway for a hardened, durable China trade regime is already drafted and could move quickly if political conditions shift — a catalyst worth monitoring in Congress.
insights.quote: The legislation is already written; what is needed now is the political will to pass it.
